guide.title: Camden, London: the British Museum, the British Library, Camden Lock and Kenwood House
guide.intro: Camden runs from Lincoln's Inn Fields north to Highgate, and its four areas hold the British Museum at Great Russell Street, the British Library at 96 Euston Road and Kenwood House on Hampstead Lane. Bloomsbury and Holborn carry four house and collection museums within a few Georgian streets. Euston Road and the railway lands behind it hold three mainline termini, Euston, St Pancras International and King's Cross, along with the British Library and the Victorian goods yard now called Coal Drops Yard. Camden Town and Chalk Farm sit on the Camden Goods Depot of 1837 and the Regent's Canal of 1812–20, with Hampstead Road Lock working between them. Hampstead and Highgate hold an Adam house, Keats House on Keats Grove, Highgate Cemetery on Swain's Lane, the Freud Museum at 20 Maresfield Gardens and the Isokon Building on Lawn Road.

sections.heading: Bloomsbury and Holborn
sections.body:
Bloomsbury and Holborn are the borough's southern tip, laid out in Georgian squares and terraces and now carrying the University of London precinct and four collections within a few streets. The British Museum fills the block behind Great Russell Street, Grade I listed, NHLE 1130404, and opens daily 10.00 to 17.00, to 20.30 on Fridays, with last entry at 16.45 and 20.15 on Fridays. Entry is free and a free advance ticket is advised; it closes 24 to 26 December. Its curtilage carries three further entries: the entrance gateway, railings and lodges at Grade II*, NHLE 1130406, eighteen forecourt lamp posts at Grade II, NHLE 1130405, and the King Edward VII Galleries at Grade I, NHLE 1322129.

Three house museums fill out the rest of a day here. Sir John Soane's Museum occupies 13 Lincoln's Inn Fields, on the north side of the square, which is in Camden; the Grade I listing, NHLE 1379327, covers Nos 12, 13 and 14 together, rebuilt in turn between about 1792 and 1824. It opens Wednesday to Sunday, 10am to 5pm, free and without pre-booking, with last admission usually at 4.30pm. The Charles Dickens Museum at 48-49 Doughty Street opens Wednesday to Sunday, 10am to 5pm, last entry 4pm, and is ticketed; Dickens lived there between 1837 and 1839 and Historic England states that the house 'is listed Grade I for this reason', NHLE 1356735. The Foundling Museum at 40 Brunswick Square opens Tuesday to Saturday 10am to 5pm and Sunday 11am to 5pm, at £14.50 for an adult, £13.50 online and free for 21 and under, and its ticket admits for a year.

The quarter sits in the Bloomsbury Conservation Area, designated by Camden as local planning authority, which carries no list entry number. Coram's Fields, on the site of the original Foundling Hospital, keeps its Grade II listed playground gates and railings, NHLE 1271627, with the forecourt gates and railings listed separately east, NHLE 1271632, and west, NHLE 1378645. The statue of Thomas Coram outside No 40 Brunswick Square is Grade II listed, NHLE 1272393.

sections.heading: Euston, King's Cross and St Pancras
sections.body:
The Euston Road spine and the railway lands behind it hold three mainline termini and two collections that charge nothing to enter. The British Library at 96 Euston Road opens Monday to Thursday 09:30 to 20:00, Friday 09:30 to 18:00, Saturday 09:30 to 17:00 and Sunday 11:00 to 17:00. Entry to the building is free, exhibitions may be ticketed, and the reading rooms need a reader pass. The library, its piazza and the boundary wall and railings to Ossulston Street, Euston Road and Midland Road were listed at Grade I on 31 July 2015, NHLE 1426345: Colin St John Wilson and M J Long's design of 1975–78, built between 1982 and 1999 and opened in 1997, on a concrete frame at 7.8m by 7.8m column centres clad in hand-made dark Victorian Red brick from Leicestershire.

The Wellcome Collection stands at 183 Euston Road, on the north side of the road opposite Euston station, and its galleries and Reading Room open Tuesday to Sunday, 10:00 to 18:00, closed Mondays. The operator states that all its permanent and temporary exhibitions, and most of its events, are free. The building itself carries no entry on the National Heritage List; the three nearest listed buildings are the UCL Chemistry Laboratory, NHLE 1322169, at 66m, No. 30 Euston Square, NHLE 1113131, at 74m, and Friends House, NHLE 1078321, at 113m.

St Pancras International and the former Midland Grand Hotel are Grade I listed together, NHLE 1342037: the station of 1865–69 and the hotel of 1868–76 by George Gilbert Scott, with William Henry Barlow's train shed of 1865–68, in deep red Gripper's patent Nottingham brick with Ancaster stone dressings and shafts of grey and red Peterhead granite. The station works; the hotel building is now a hotel and apartments and is publicly accessible only in part. Behind it, Coal Drops Yard is a shopping and eating quarter in the Eastern Coal Drops of 1851–52, Grade II listed, NHLE 1379214, beside Lewis Cubitt's Granary of the same years, Grade II listed, NHLE 1379215, which houses Central Saint Martins and is not generally open to visitors. Gasholder No. 8 of 1883, Grade II listed, NHLE 1423467, was re-erected around a park in 2014, and the Triplet of 1879–80, Grade II listed, NHLE 1464325, around apartment blocks in 2018. The King's Cross and St Pancras Conservation Area and the Regent's Canal Conservation Area, both designated by Camden as local planning authority, cover this ground and carry no list entry numbers.

sections.heading: Camden Town and Chalk Farm
sections.body:
Camden Town and Chalk Farm are built on the Camden Goods Depot, which Robert Stephenson began in 1837 on a 25-acre site bought from Lord Southampton and opened to traffic in 1839. Camden Market occupies it now, at Camden Lock Place, open Monday to Sunday 10am to 7pm including bank holidays, with the Hawley Wharf food halls at Chalk Farm Road open 11.30am to 11pm; the operator notes that individual times may vary, since the market is made up of independent businesses. The depot's structures stand around the stalls. The Interchange, Grade II listed, NHLE 1113238, is a four-storey warehouse built directly over the canal basin, its ground floor carried on a line of octagonal steel columns down the centre of the basin. The Horse Hospital, Grade II* listed, NHLE 1258100, held 92 horses in its western range of 1882–83 and 40 more in the eastern range of 1897. The Stanley Sidings stables are Grade II listed, NHLE 1258101.

Hampstead Road Lock, also called Camden Lock, works on the Regent's Canal at Chalk Farm Road and is freely accessible from the towpath. It is Grade II listed, NHLE 1272427, listed on 9 January 1992, and stands in the Regent's Canal Conservation Area, designated by Camden as local planning authority, which carries no list entry number. The roving bridge over the canal west of the lock, NHLE 1272428, the Hampstead Road bridge over the canal, NHLE 1272426, and the Regent's Canal Information Centre beside the lock, NHLE 1244300, are all Grade II listed. The canal was built between 1812 and 1820, and it is why Stephenson put the depot here: it gave the railway a freight link to the London docks.

The Roundhouse on Chalk Farm Road is a goods locomotive shed of 1846–47 by Robert B Dockray, built by Branson & Gwyther, Grade II* listed, NHLE 1258103, and listed on 10 June 1954 under the name 'The Round House Theatre'. It works as a performance venue and admits by event ticket, so a visit follows the programme rather than an opening time. A cattle trough opposite the debouchment of Belmont Street, NHLE 1258104, and a drinking fountain set in the wall next to the Roundhouse, NHLE 1258105, are Grade II listed. On Gloucester Avenue, the Camden Incline Winding Engine House of 1837 by Robert Stephenson is Grade II* listed, NHLE 1342073, with four parallel vaulted underground chambers each about 35m long.

sections.heading: Hampstead and Highgate
sections.body:
Hampstead and Highgate are the high northern villages either side of Hampstead Heath, and Camden's five places here stand on and around the Heath, which itself runs on into Barnet and Haringey. Kenwood House on Hampstead Lane opens daily 10am to 5pm with last entry at 4.30pm, free, run by English Heritage: a core of about 1616 remodelled by Robert and James Adam between about 1764 and 1779, Grade I listed, NHLE 1379242, in grounds on the Register of Historic Parks and Gardens at Grade II*, NHLE 1000142, 47.0 hectares registered on 1 October 1987. The Iveagh Bequest hangs Rembrandt's 'Self-Portrait with Two Circles' there, and the operator names Vermeer, Gainsborough, Turner and Constable in the collection.

Keats House at 10 Keats Grove is the pair of about 1815–16 once known as Wentworth Place, Grade I listed, NHLE 1379221, and run by the City of London Corporation. It is ticketed, and volunteer-led ground-floor tours run most Thursday, Friday and Sunday afternoons from about 2.15pm, last about 30 minutes and carry no extra charge. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here. The Freud Museum London at 20 Maresfield Gardens opens Wednesday to Sunday 10:30 to 17:00, at £16.90 for an adult with donation and £14.90 without, in a house Grade II listed as '20, MARESFIELD GARDENS', NHLE 1113113. The Isokon Building on Lawn Road, Wells Coates's block of 36 flats built in 1933–34, is Grade I listed, NHLE 1379280, and is lived in, so it is seen from the street; the small volunteer-run gallery in its former garage publishes no hours that a source states, so none are given here.

Highgate Cemetery on Swain's Lane opens daily 10am to 5pm from March to October, last entry 4.30pm, and daily 10am to 4pm from November to February, last entry 3.30pm, closed Christmas Day and Boxing Day. Visits are ticketed and it is still a working burial ground. It is on the Register of Historic Parks and Gardens at Grade I, NHLE 1000810, 14.7 hectares. The London Cemetery Company opened it in 1839 on 17.5 acres and doubled it in 1854 with the East Cemetery extension across Swain's Lane; by 1888 it held more than 25,000 graves. The Egyptian Avenue of about 1838–39 and the Lebanon Circle are Grade I listed, NHLE 1271935, and the Terrace Catacombs of 1838–39 are Grade II* listed, NHLE 1378923.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
All three mainline termini are inside the borough. For London St Pancras International take East Midlands Railway, Hull Trains, Southeastern or Thameslink. For London King's Cross take Grand Central, Great Northern, Hull Trains, London North Eastern Railway, Lumo or Thameslink. For London Euston take Avanti West Coast, West Midlands Trains or the Lioness Overground line. The interchange to aim for is King's Cross St. Pancras Underground station, which carries the Circle, Hammersmith & City, Metropolitan, Northern, Piccadilly and Victoria lines.

Eight Underground lines serve stations inside the borough: Central at Holborn and Chancery Lane; Circle, Hammersmith & City and Metropolitan at King's Cross St. Pancras and Euston Square, with the Metropolitan also at Finchley Road; Jubilee at Swiss Cottage and Finchley Road; and the Northern, Piccadilly and Victoria lines. Two Overground lines run through it, the Mildmay and the Lioness at Euston. Tottenham Court Road, the nearest Elizabeth line station, straddles the Camden and Westminster boundary: TfL's station point and the Dean Street ticket hall fall in Westminster, and the Centre Point end falls in Camden.

For Bloomsbury and Holborn, catch the Piccadilly line to Russell Square for the British Museum and the Foundling Museum, the Central or Piccadilly line to Holborn for Sir John Soane's Museum, and the Central line to Chancery Lane for Doughty Street. Goodge Street on the Northern line serves the western end. For Camden Town and Chalk Farm, catch the Northern line to Camden Town or Chalk Farm, or the Mildmay Overground to Camden Road for the market and to Kentish Town West for the Roundhouse; the 1, 88, 214, 253 and 274 buses stop at Camden Town Station / Bayham Street. For Hampstead and Highgate, catch the Northern line to Hampstead or Highgate for Kenwood House, the Mildmay Overground to Hampstead Heath for Keats House and the Isokon Building, and the Jubilee or Metropolitan line to Finchley Road for the Freud Museum, about 250m away. Belsize Park on the Northern line also serves the Isokon Building. Highgate and Archway, the closest stations to Highgate Cemetery, are in Haringey and Islington. Kenwood House has no station within 500m: Highgate, Hampstead and Hampstead Heath are each roughly 1.5 to 1.8km away across the Heath.

faq.question: What does the British Museum cost, and when is it open?
faq.answer: Entry is free and a free advance ticket is advised. It opens daily 10.00 to 17.00 and to 20.30 on Fridays, with last entry at 16.45 and at 20.15 on Fridays, and it closes 24 to 26 December. The address is Great Russell Street, London WC1B 3DG. Sir Robert Smirke built it in Portland stone between 1823 and 1847, and it is Grade I listed, NHLE 1130404.

faq.question: Are Regent's Park and London Zoo in Camden?
faq.answer: No. ZSL London Zoo at Outer Circle, NW1 4RY, its main entrance, the boating lake and the Inner Circle all resolve to the City of Westminster, and Regent's Park itself is a Westminster park. Only the zoo's northern and eastern fringe along the Outer Circle falls in the London Borough of Camden. Primrose Hill, north-east of the park, is in Camden.

faq.question: What does Highgate Cemetery cost, and when is it open?
faq.answer: It opens daily 10am to 5pm from March to October, with last entry at 4.30pm, and daily 10am to 4pm from November to February, with last entry at 3.30pm, and closes on Christmas Day and Boxing Day. Visits are ticketed. No source states a standard single-visitor adult admission price, so none is given here; the operator does publish group visits at a minimum of £100 for ten or more, and private tours at £18 for an adult, £9 for a child aged 8 to 17 and £9.50 for a student. There is no on-site visitor parking.

faq.question: Which houses in Camden can be gone into, and when?
faq.answer: Sir John Soane's Museum at 13 Lincoln's Inn Fields opens Wednesday to Sunday 10am to 5pm, free. The Charles Dickens Museum at 48-49 Doughty Street opens Wednesday to Sunday 10am to 5pm, ticketed. The Foundling Museum at 40 Brunswick Square opens Tuesday to Saturday 10am to 5pm and Sunday 11am to 5pm. The Freud Museum at 20 Maresfield Gardens opens Wednesday to Sunday 10:30 to 17:00. Kenwood House opens daily 10am to 5pm, free. Keats House is ticketed but no source states its hours, so none are given here, and the Isokon Building is lived in, so it is seen from the street.

faq.question: What is Camden Lock, and can it be walked to from the market?
faq.answer: Camden Lock is Hampstead Road Lock, a working lock on the Regent's Canal at Chalk Farm Road, freely accessible from the towpath. It is Grade II listed, NHLE 1272427, listed on 9 January 1992, and it stands in the Regent's Canal Conservation Area, designated by Camden as local planning authority, which carries no list entry number. Camden Market occupies the Camden Goods Depot beside it, at Camden Lock Place, open 10am to 7pm daily. Camden Town and Chalk Farm on the Northern line serve both.

faq.question: Which stations serve the borough's mainline termini?
faq.answer: Euston, St Pancras International and King's Cross are all inside Camden. King's Cross St. Pancras Underground station carries the Circle, Hammersmith & City, Metropolitan, Northern, Piccadilly and Victoria lines. Euston Underground station carries the Northern and Victoria lines, Euston Square carries the Circle, Hammersmith & City and Metropolitan lines, and the Lioness Overground line runs from Euston. St Pancras International is served by East Midlands Railway, Hull Trains, Southeastern and Thameslink.

places.name: The British Museum
places.summary: The British Museum stands on Great Russell Street in Bloomsbury. It opens daily 10.00 to 17.00 and to 20.30 on Fridays, with last entry at 16.45 and at 20.15 on Fridays, and closes 24 to 26 December. Entry is free and a free advance ticket is advised. The building is Grade I listed, NHLE 1130404, and stands in the Bloomsbury Conservation Area, designated by Camden as local planning authority, which carries no list entry number.
places.history: Sir Robert Smirke built the museum in Portland stone between 1823 and 1847, planning it as a quadrangle extending north from Montague House, which was demolished around 1840 (NHLE 1130404). The South Range of 1842–47 carries an Ionic octastyle portico whose order is copied from the temple of Athene Polias at Priene, and the pediment sculpture is Westmacott's 'Progress of Civilisation'. The East Wing of 1823–26 used iron beams clad in concrete by the engineer John Rastrick, an early instance of the technique. Sydney Smirke's Round Reading Room of 1852–57 was put up to fill the open quadrangle and has a domed cast-iron roof. Three further entries on the National Heritage List cover the curtilage separately: the main entrance gateway, railings and lodges at Grade II*, NHLE 1130406; eighteen forecourt lamp posts at Grade II, NHLE 1130405; and the King Edward VII Galleries at Grade I, NHLE 1322129.

places.name: Sir John Soane's Museum
places.summary: Sir John Soane's Museum occupies 13 Lincoln's Inn Fields, on the north side of the square, which is in the London Borough of Camden. The operator gives normal opening as Wednesday to Sunday, 10am to 5pm, with last admission usually at 4.30pm and admissions closed earlier if the museum reaches capacity; it closes Monday and Tuesday but opens on bank holidays. Entry is free and no pre-booking is required. Free volunteer-led tours of the Private Apartments run Wednesday, Friday and Sunday at 2pm for up to eight people, and of the Drawing Office on Thursday and Saturday at 2.30pm for up to six.
places.history: The Grade I listing, NHLE 1379327, covers three terraced houses — Nos 12, 13 and 14 Lincoln's Inn Fields — which Soane rebuilt in turn into a single symmetrical facade: No 12 in about 1792–94, No 13 in about 1812–13 and No 14 in about 1824. Soane built the museum itself on the site of the stables behind No 13; No 14 was sold off, but its back half was retained and absorbed into the principal residence. The Drawing Office opened to the public in May 2023. Soane's tomb for his wife and son, in St Pancras Old Church Gardens elsewhere in the borough, is Grade I listed, NHLE 1322044, and Historic England records its domed form as the influence on Giles Gilbert Scott's K2 telephone kiosk.

places.name: Charles Dickens Museum
places.summary: The Charles Dickens Museum occupies 48-49 Doughty Street and opens Wednesday to Sunday, 10am to 5pm, with last entry at 4pm. It is ticketed. The house is a terrace of about 1807–09 in darkened stock brick with a slate mansard roof, of three storeys plus attic and basement, and it is Grade I listed, NHLE 1356735.
places.history: Dickens lived here between 1837 and 1839, and the Historic England entry states that the house 'is listed Grade I for this reason' — the grade rests on the historic association rather than on the architecture (NHLE 1356735). The entry was formerly part of the group 'Nos.39-62 (Consecutive) Doughty Street' before being separated out. The house keeps its original lead rainwater head and pipe and the attached cast-iron railings with urn finials to the areas.

places.name: The Foundling Museum
places.summary: The Foundling Museum is at 40 Brunswick Square and opens Tuesday to Saturday 10am to 5pm and Sunday 11am to 5pm, closed Mondays. Admission is £14.50 for an adult, £13.50 online, and free for 21 and under, for members and for care-experienced individuals; a ticket gives free entry for a year. The building is Grade II listed as 'No.40 Thomas Coram Foundation for Children and attached railings, lanterns & parapets', NHLE 1272392.
places.history: The present building is a detached Neo-Georgian office block of about 1937 by J M Shepherd for the Thomas Coram Foundation, in brown brick with a hipped pantile roof; a central stone plaque at second-floor level is inscribed 'RFTHG 1937' (NHLE 1272392). The doorway carries a scrolled pediment with a central bust of Coram, flanked at first-floor level by roundels of putti heads carved in low relief. The collection includes 'Moses Brought Before Pharaoh's Daughter', which the operator records Hogarth presenting to the Hospital on 1 April 1747. The site of the original Foundling Hospital is now Coram's Fields, next door: the playground with its gates and railings is Grade II listed, NHLE 1271627, with the forecourt gates and railings listed separately east, NHLE 1271632, and west, NHLE 1378645. The statue of Thomas Coram outside No 40 is Grade II listed, NHLE 1272393.

places.name: The British Library
places.summary: The British Library is at 96 Euston Road and opens Monday to Thursday 09:30 to 20:00, Friday 09:30 to 18:00, Saturday 09:30 to 17:00 and Sunday 11:00 to 17:00. Entry to the building is free; exhibitions may be ticketed, and the reading rooms need a reader pass. The library, its piazza and the boundary wall and railings to Ossulston Street, Euston Road and Midland Road were listed at Grade I on 31 July 2015, NHLE 1426345.
places.history: Sir Colin St John Wilson designed the library with M J Long. The built design follows the scheme of 1975–78, construction ran from 1982 to 1999 and the building opened in 1997 (NHLE 1426345). It has a concrete frame on 7.8m by 7.8m column centres, clad inside and out in hand-made sand-faced dark Victorian Red brick from Leicestershire, chosen because it comes from the same clay as the bricks of St Pancras Station and Hotel next door. Ove Arup and Partners were the structural engineers. The listing takes in works of art integral to the design and names Paolozzi's 'Newton' in the piazza, while excluding free-standing or curated works; the adjoining Conservation Centre of 2006, by Long and Kentish, is stated not to form part of the special interest. The library's origin is the Royal Library of 10,500 volumes presented by George II in 1757, which brought with it the right to a copy of every book entered at Stationers' Hall; the Copyright Act 1911 extended that to every book, periodical and newspaper published in Britain.

places.name: Wellcome Collection
places.summary: The Wellcome Collection is at 183 Euston Road, on the north side of the road opposite Euston station. Its galleries and Reading Room open Tuesday to Sunday, 10:00 to 18:00, and close on Mondays. The operator states that all its permanent and temporary exhibitions, and most of its events, are free, and publishes separate opening times for the Library, the café and the shop. The telephone number is +44 (0)20 7611 2222.
places.history: The public museum and library of the history of medicine opened on this site in 2007. The Wellcome Building carries no entry on the National Heritage List of its own; the three nearest listed buildings are the UCL Chemistry Laboratory, NHLE 1322169, at 66m, No. 30 Euston Square, NHLE 1113131, at 74m, and Friends House, NHLE 1078321, at 113m. The site stands in the Bloomsbury Conservation Area, designated by Camden as local planning authority, which carries no list entry number.

places.name: St Pancras International and the former Midland Grand Hotel
places.summary: St Pancras International is a working railway station on Euston Road, with the former Midland Grand Hotel across its front. The station of 1865–69 and the hotel of 1868–76 are Grade I listed together, NHLE 1342037. The hotel building is now a hotel and apartments and is publicly accessible only in part.
places.history: George Gilbert Scott designed both the station and the Midland Grand Hotel; the train shed of 1865–68 is by the engineer William Henry Barlow (NHLE 1342037). It is built in deep red Gripper's patent Nottingham brick with Ancaster stone dressings and shafts of grey and red Peterhead granite, and the slated roofs were renewed in 1994 in carefully diminishing courses. The Gothic Revival frontage is of 23 windows flanked by towers, with a curved 10-window wing. The listing covers the train shed, terminus facilities, offices, ancillary buildings, taxi stand, warehousing, substructure and forecourt structures, not the hotel front alone. A K6 telephone kiosk outside the station is Grade II listed, NHLE 1393675. The site lies in the King's Cross and St Pancras Conservation Area, designated by Camden as local planning authority, which carries no list entry number.

places.name: Coal Drops Yard and the Granary
places.address: Stable Street, Granary Square, London N1C 4DQ
places.summary: Coal Drops Yard is a public shopping and eating quarter at Stable Street, off Granary Square. Individual traders set their own hours and no source states a single opening time for the quarter, so none is given here. The Eastern Coal Drops are Grade II listed, NHLE 1379214, and the Granary is Grade II listed, NHLE 1379215; the Granary houses Central Saint Martins and is not generally open to visitors.
places.history: The Eastern Coal Drops were built in 1851–52, probably by Lewis Cubitt, in multi-coloured stock brick over a framework of cast-iron columns and beams; the northern coal-handling bays were damaged by fire in 1985 (NHLE 1379214). The Granary is by Lewis Cubitt, 1851–52, of six storeys, with a symmetrical nine-bay south front, four projecting hoist bays and 46 cast-iron columns to each floor (NHLE 1379215). Gasholder No. 8, Grade II listed, NHLE 1423467, is a guide frame of 1883 by the engineer John Clark; it was moved about 300m from the St Pancras gasworks, dismantled around 2001, restored by Shepley Engineers and re-erected around a park in 2014. The Triplet — Gasholder Nos 10, 11 and 12, Grade II listed, NHLE 1464325 — is three conjoined guide frames of 1879–80, each about 33m high, of 15 columns and 40.8m diameter, 16 columns and 44.3m, and 13 columns and 32.3m; the columns run Tuscan, Doric then simplified Corinthian from bottom to top, and the frames were re-erected around apartment blocks in 2018. The St Pancras gasworks stayed active until 1904. The steam locomotive water point, NHLE 1113023, and the canal-side lock keeper's cottage and former pumping house, NHLE 1272512, are both Grade II listed. The site lies in the Regent's Canal Conservation Area, designated by Camden as local planning authority, which carries no list entry number.

places.name: Camden Market
places.summary: Camden Market is at Camden Lock Place and opens Monday to Sunday, 10am to 7pm, including bank holidays; the Hawley Wharf food halls open Monday to Sunday, 11.30am to 11pm. The operator notes that individual times may vary, since the market is made up of independent businesses. A second address, Hawley Wharf, is at Chalk Farm Road, London NW1 8AA.
places.history: The market occupies the Camden Goods Depot, built from 1837 as the London terminus for goods traffic on the London and Birmingham Railway. Robert Stephenson chose the 25-acre site north of the canal, bought from Lord Southampton in January 1837, because it let freight interconnect with the London docks by way of the Regent's Canal of 1812–20; the depot opened to traffic in 1839 (NHLE 1113238). The Interchange, Grade II listed, NHLE 1113238, is a four-storey warehouse built directly over the canal basin, its ground floor carried on a line of octagonal steel columns down the centre of the basin, with 24 window bays to the long east and west elevations. The Horse Hospital, Grade II* listed, NHLE 1258100, is of two phases: the western range of 1882–83 held 92 horses over two storeys and the eastern range of 1897 a further 40. The Stanley Sidings stables are Grade II listed, NHLE 1258101. The original depot included 18 coke ovens for making smokeless locomotive fuel and stabling for 50 horses.

places.name: The Roundhouse
places.summary: The Roundhouse is a performance venue on Chalk Farm Road. Entry is by event ticket and the operator publishes no general daytime admission, so no opening hours are given here. The building is Grade II* listed, NHLE 1258103, and was listed on 10 June 1954 under the name 'The Round House Theatre'.
places.history: It was built in 1846–47 as a goods locomotive shed, designed by Robert B Dockray for the London and North Western Railway and built by Branson & Gwyther (NHLE 1258103). It later served as a warehouse for W & A Gilbey Ltd, and was converted for use as a theatre in 1967 and again in 1985. The engine house was one of two put up in the 1846–48 overhaul of the goods depot; its counterpart for passenger engines, south of the main line, was demolished in 1966 (NHLE 1258100). Two further Grade II entries stand immediately outside: a cattle trough opposite the debouchment of Belmont Street, NHLE 1258104, and a drinking fountain set in the wall next to the Roundhouse, NHLE 1258105. On Gloucester Avenue, the Camden Incline Winding Engine House of 1837 by Robert Stephenson is Grade II* listed, NHLE 1342073: four parallel vaulted underground chambers, each about 35m long, 4.5m wide and 7m high, with a larger transverse vault at the north-west end, about 23m by 9m and 5.5m high, which housed the twin 60 horsepower condensing engines and the 20-foot-diameter drive wheel that hauled trains up the incline from Euston.

places.name: Hampstead Road Lock (Camden Lock)
places.address: Regent's Canal at Chalk Farm Road, London NW1 8AB
places.summary: Hampstead Road Lock, also called Camden Lock, is a working lock on the Regent's Canal at Chalk Farm Road, freely accessible from the towpath. It is Grade II listed, NHLE 1272427, and was listed on 9 January 1992. No source states opening hours for it, so none are given here.
places.history: The Regent's Canal was built between 1812 and 1820, and it is why Robert Stephenson sited the Camden Goods Depot here: it gave the railway a freight link to the London docks (NHLE 1113238). The roving bridge over the canal west of the lock is Grade II listed, NHLE 1272428, as is the Hampstead Road bridge over the canal, NHLE 1272426. The Regent's Canal Information Centre beside the lock is Grade II listed, NHLE 1244300. The lock stands in the Regent's Canal Conservation Area, designated by Camden as local planning authority, which carries no list entry number.

places.name: Kenwood House
places.summary: Kenwood House stands on Hampstead Lane and is run by English Heritage. The house opens daily 10am to 5pm, with last entry at 4.30pm; entry is free and online booking is optional. The house is Grade I listed, NHLE 1379242, and its grounds are on the Register of Historic Parks and Gardens at Grade II*, NHLE 1000142, registered on 1 October 1987 and covering 47.0 hectares. The operator invites visitors to 'roam 112 acres of glorious parkland designed by Humphry Repton'.
places.history: The core of the present house was built about 1616 and renovated about 1749, when the orangery and boudoir were added to the west (NHLE 1379242). Robert and James Adam worked here between about 1764 and 1779, remodelling the south front with a second storey and adding the library with its anteroom to the east and the north entrance portico. George Saunders added the projecting north wings and the west veranda about 1795, together with the service wing and kitchens, which are listed separately at Grade II*, NHLE 1379244. The house was restored between 1955 and 1959. The registered landscape is a mid-eighteenth-century park with lakes and woodland, developed further in the late eighteenth century by Humphry Repton, William Marshall and William Emes; a lime avenue running west from the south front was planted about 1726 by George Middleton (NHLE 1000142). The estate carries many separate Grade II listings, among them the East Lodge and gateways, NHLE 1378705, West Lodge, NHLE 1378708, the former dairy buildings, NHLE 1379243, and the 'Monolith (Empyrean)' sculpture in the grounds, NHLE 1378710; the Sham Bridge south of the house is Grade II* listed, NHLE 1379245. The Iveagh Bequest collection includes Rembrandt's 'Self-Portrait with Two Circles', and the operator names Vermeer, Gainsborough, Turner and Constable in the collection.

places.name: Keats House
places.summary: Keats House is at 10 Keats Grove and is run by the City of London Corporation. It is ticketed. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here. Volunteer-led tours of the ground floor run most Thursday, Friday and Sunday afternoons from about 2.15pm, last about 30 minutes and carry no extra charge. The house is Grade I listed, NHLE 1379221, and was listed on 11 August 1950.
places.history: It was built in about 1815–16 as a semi-detached pair designed to look like one house, then known as Wentworth Place, and was later converted into a single house museum (NHLE 1379221). It was built for the antiquary and critic Charles Wentworth Dilke and the writer Charles Armitage Brown, and altered about 1839 and again in the late twentieth century. It is stuccoed, with a slated hipped roof, projecting eaves and tall chimney-stacks on both returns; two storeys and a basement, double-fronted with three windows, plus a single-storey two-window extension at the east end added about 1839–40. The neighbouring Keats Community Library is Grade II listed, NHLE 1430883, and Nos 1, 2, 3, 4 and 12 Keats Grove are each Grade II listed in their own right. Hampstead Heath is in Camden at this point.

places.name: Highgate Cemetery
places.summary: Highgate Cemetery is on Swain's Lane and is still a working burial ground. It opens daily 10am to 5pm from March to October, with last entry at 4.30pm, and daily 10am to 4pm from November to February, with last entry at 3.30pm; it closes on Christmas Day and Boxing Day. Visits are ticketed and there is no on-site visitor parking. The cemetery is on the Register of Historic Parks and Gardens at Grade I, NHLE 1000810, registered on 1 October 1987 and covering 14.7 hectares.
places.history: The London Cemetery Company, founded in 1836 by the architect and civil engineer Stephen Geary, laid the ground out and opened it in 1839 as the Cemetery of St James; the Bishop of London consecrated it in May 1839 (NHLE 1000810). The original site was 17.5 acres, about 7.3 hectares, and took in part of the grounds of Ashurst Manor, once owned by Sir William Ashurst, Lord Mayor of London in 1693. It doubled in size in 1854 with the East Cemetery extension across Swain's Lane, connected to the west side by a passage under the lane so that coffins could be carried from the chapel to the graves. By 1888 there were more than 25,000 graves, with an average of four bodies each. The Egyptian Avenue of about 1838–39, probably by J B Bunning, is an avenue of catacombs cut into the hillside and built in false perspective to appear longer than it is; the outer ring of the Lebanon Circle is by Thomas Porter, about 1870. Both are Grade I listed, NHLE 1271935. The Terrace Catacombs of 1838–39 are Grade II* listed, NHLE 1378923. Individual monuments carry their own entries, among them the Grade II* Julius Beer mausoleum, NHLE 1378887, and the Grade II tombs of Michael Faraday, NHLE 1378950, of Christina Rossetti and Elizabeth Siddall, NHLE 1378931, and of the Dickens family, NHLE 1378894. The Friends of Highgate Cemetery Trust states that it receives virtually no government funding and that 'it costs at least £1.4 million a year to keep the Cemetery open'.

places.name: Freud Museum London
places.summary: The Freud Museum London is at 20 Maresfield Gardens and opens Wednesday to Sunday, 10:30 to 17:00, closed Monday and Tuesday. Admission is £16.90 for an adult with donation and £14.90 without; audio guides and exhibitions are included, and visitors are asked to bring their own headphones. The house is Grade II listed as '20, MARESFIELD GARDENS', NHLE 1113113.
places.history: The neighbouring British College of Naturopathy and Osteopathy is Grade II listed, NHLE 1322103. Oscar Nemon's seated bronze 'Sigmund Freud' of about 1970 is Grade II listed, NHLE 1431355; Historic England places it at the junction of Fitzjohn's Avenue and Belsize Lane, in the grounds of the Tavistock Clinic, 'near Freud's last home in Maresfield Gardens', about 270m south-south-east of the museum. Measured from the listed-building point, Finchley Road station is about 250m away, Finchley Road & Frognal about 450m and Swiss Cottage about 550m.

places.name: Isokon Building (Lawn Road Flats)
places.summary: The Isokon Building, also known as the Lawn Road Flats, is a private residential block on Lawn Road, seen from the street. A small volunteer-run gallery occupies the former garage; no source states its opening hours, so none are given here. The building is Grade I listed as 'Numbers I, 1A, 1B, 1C and 1D and 2-32 Isokon Flats', NHLE 1379280, and was listed on 14 May 1974.
places.history: Wells Coates designed the block of 36 flats between 1929 and 1932 and it was built in 1933–34 for Jack and Molly Pritchard, using the Pritchards' Venesta plywood products (NHLE 1379280). It is a monolithic reinforced-concrete structure with a cement wash applied direct to the concrete, a flat roof and metal windows, of four storeys plus a penthouse. Each floor held six one-room 'minimum' flats, two of them with balconies, plus a studio with a balcony and a one-bedroom flat, with a penthouse for the Pritchards and a separate one for their children on the roof. The flats were conceived as a cheap but independent alternative to lodgings, with space-saving fitted furniture and closets, and most keep their original Coates fitted kitchens, dressing rooms and bathrooms. Marcel Breuer and F R S Yorke converted the ground-floor kitchens and staff flat into the Isobar in 1937. The building stands in the Parkhill Conservation Area, designated by Camden as local planning authority, which carries no list entry number.

links.note: The Regent's Canal runs east from Hampstead Road Lock to Islington's City Road Basin and the Islington Tunnel.
Sir John Soane's Museum stands at Lincoln's Inn Fields; Soane also built the Bank of England, whose museum is in the City.
Bloomsbury's British Museum and British Library against South Kensington's V&A, Natural History Museum and Science Museum.

entries.name: The British Museum
entries.note: Free entry on Great Russell Street, daily 10.00 to 17.00 and to 20.30 on Fridays; a free advance ticket is advised and it closes 24 to 26 December.

entries.name: Sir John Soane's Museum
entries.note: Three houses at Lincoln's Inn Fields rebuilt by Soane between about 1792 and 1824, open Wednesday to Sunday 10am to 5pm, free and without pre-booking.

entries.name: The Private Apartments and Drawing Office at Soane's
entries.note: Free volunteer-led tours: the Private Apartments Wednesday, Friday and Sunday at 2pm for eight people, the Drawing Office Thursday and Saturday at 2.30pm for six.

entries.name: Charles Dickens Museum
entries.note: The Doughty Street house Dickens lived in from 1837 to 1839, ticketed, open Wednesday to Sunday 10am to 5pm with last entry at 4pm.

entries.name: The Foundling Museum
entries.note: £14.50 for an adult and free for 21 and under, with the ticket valid a year; Tuesday to Saturday 10am to 5pm, Sunday 11am to 5pm.

entries.name: The British Library
entries.note: Free to enter at 96 Euston Road, Monday to Thursday 09:30 to 20:00 and shorter at the weekend; exhibitions may be ticketed and reading rooms need a pass.

entries.name: Wellcome Collection
entries.note: Galleries and Reading Room Tuesday to Sunday 10:00 to 18:00, closed Mondays; the operator states its exhibitions and most events are free.

entries.name: St Pancras International
entries.note: George Gilbert Scott's station of 1865–69 and Midland Grand Hotel of 1868–76, Grade I listed together, NHLE 1342037, with Barlow's train shed of 1865–68.

entries.name: Coal Drops Yard
entries.note: Eating and shopping in the coal drops of 1851–52 at Stable Street; traders set their own hours, and the Granary next door houses Central Saint Martins.

entries.name: Camden Market and Hawley Wharf
entries.note: Camden Lock Place 10am to 7pm daily including bank holidays; the Hawley Wharf food halls at Chalk Farm Road run 11.30am to 11pm.

entries.name: The Roundhouse
entries.note: An 1846–47 goods locomotive shed working as a venue; entry is by event ticket, so check the programme before walking up Chalk Farm Road.

entries.name: Hampstead Road Lock
entries.note: A working lock on the Regent's Canal, freely accessible from the towpath, with the roving bridge and the Hampstead Road bridge either side of it.

entries.name: Kenwood House
entries.note: Free, daily 10am to 5pm with last entry 4.30pm: an Adam interior of about 1764–79 and the Iveagh Bequest, in 47.0 hectares of registered landscape, NHLE 1000142.

entries.name: Keats House ground-floor tour
entries.note: Volunteer-led tours most Thursday, Friday and Sunday afternoons from about 2.15pm, about 30 minutes, at no extra charge above the ticket.

entries.name: Highgate Cemetery
entries.note: Ticketed, 10am to 5pm March to October and 10am to 4pm November to February; the Egyptian Avenue and Lebanon Circle are Grade I listed, NHLE 1271935.

entries.name: Freud Museum London
entries.note: 20 Maresfield Gardens, Wednesday to Sunday 10:30 to 17:00, £16.90 with donation or £14.90 without; bring headphones for the audio guide.

entries.name: Isokon Building
entries.note: Wells Coates's 36 reinforced-concrete flats of 1933–34 on Lawn Road, Grade I listed, NHLE 1379280, lived in and seen from the street.
